record.aspect_adaptations: All 10 aspects apply with two honest adaptations: concurrency is read as parallel build and parallel test semantics (declared DEPENDS edges as the correctness condition, job pools as the budget, CTest RESOURCE_LOCK and fixtures under -j); memory_ownership is read as target and artifact discipline (who owns each target, generated file and build directory, configure-time cost and cache retention as the bounded resources, the disposable build directory as the lifetime unit). static_analysis is the language-server pairing (neocmakelsp) plus configure-time policy, CMake having no separate linter in the guide's toolchain.

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the documented command set: message levels, DEFINED-vs-truthiness separation under if(), and the documented false-constant list are all as the guide states them, and failing the configure is the only enforcement a build description has. assertions_contracts.guide_position: CMake has no assertion statement, so the assertion is an explicit check that fails the configure: message(FATAL_ERROR) for a violated precondition with the variable named, its actual value and the legal values; message(SEND_ERROR) when several independent problems should be reported in one pass with generation still suppressed; validation happens early, at the boundary where the bad value enters; existence is guarded before value (if(NOT DEFINED VAR) first) because if() on an undefined variable is silently false; postconditions are properties of the generated graph (sources exist on disk, exported targets name their export set, every test has a timeout) checked by the validation recipes.

bounded_work.best_practice: No Kitware source contradicts the bounds; the mechanisms the guide binds (test TIMEOUT, execute_process TIMEOUT, job pools, hash-pinned downloads) are the documented ones, and banning file(GLOB) for sources reflects the documented configure-time evaluation of glob results. Stricter than mainstream practice by design.

bounded_work.guide_position: Explicit source lists and file sets only (file(GLOB) banned for sources; CONFIGURE_DEPENDS is the named, commented exception); a TIMEOUT on every add_test and every execute_process; downloads pinned by URL_HASH or full commit hash; compile and link job pools bounding peak parallel memory; generated files declared as bounded OUTPUT/BYPRODUCTS with real DEPENDS edges and nothing generated into the source tree; the supported configuration space is the committed preset list, not the cross product of every cache variable; a failed configure is fixed at the input and re-run from the same preset, never retried as a strategy.

concurrency.best_practice: Consistent with the documented build model: the generator schedules from the declared graph, job pools are the documented memory-bounding mechanism for Ninja, and CTest's RESOURCE_LOCK and FIXTURES_* properties are the documented tools for exclusive resources and ordered setup under parallel test runs.
concurrency.evidence: Guide sections 14, 16 and 21 state the dependency-edge rule, the pool mechanism and the CTest contracts together, so a parallel build's correctness claim rests on declared edges rather than on build order.
concurrency.guide_position: CMake configures serially, so concurrency lives in the generated build and the test run, and both are correct only when dependencies are declared: any file target B reads from target A's build is a target-level dependency (target_link_libraries, add_dependencies, or an OBJECT/INTERFACE carrier), never preset build order or a comment; named job pools defined in the root listfile (CMAKE_JOB_POOL_COMPILE/LINK or per-target assignment) bound peak memory, with the link pool as the usual ceiling; ExternalProject steps that share a prefix need explicit step dependencies or separate prefixes; under ctest -j, exclusive resources declare RESOURCE_LOCK and fixture pairs use FIXTURES_SETUP/CLEANUP/REQUIRED; test processes that spawn grandchildren own reaping them.

error_handling.best_practice: The message-level discipline and call-site result checking match the documented behavior of message, execute_process, try_compile/try_run and find_package; execute_process even documents COMMAND_ERROR_IS_FATAL (since 3.19), which complements rather than replaces the guide's checked-result pattern where the captured output must appear in the error message.
error_handling.evidence: Guide sections 7 and 20 state the level discipline, the immediate result check with the command line in scope for the message, and the three distinct failure kinds (exit code, signal string, not started).
error_handling.guide_position: Configure-time errors are the build system's type errors, caught where the bad value enters: FATAL_ERROR stops because the graph cannot be trusted, SEND_ERROR records and suppresses generation, WARNING is reserved for deprecations and surprising-but-legal states (a warning that fires every configure will be ignored), STATUS/VERBOSE/DEBUG carry progress and diagnostics; every execute_process result is checked immediately at the call site and a failure names the command line, the result and the captured output; try_compile/try_run results are variables and an unchecked one is an unhandled error; find_package(... REQUIRED) failing is the error handling, with optional packages decided in exactly one place via <pkg>_FOUND; error messages name the variable to change, the value found and the constraint violated.

memory_ownership.best_practice: No official source contradicts the ownership model; the bounded-inspection route the guide prefers (the CMake file API) over parsing CMakeCache.txt or generated build files is the documented external interface, and treating the cache as user input is the documented consequence of its persistence semantics.

memory_ownership.guide_position: State has four owners: normal variables (the default), the cache (the build directory's persistent, public, user-input surface: typed, docstringed, never hand-edited, and a stale cache is deleted with its whole directory rather than surgically patched), properties (attached state with a named owner; global properties are append-only registries owned by one module), and the filesystem (generated files under the binary dir, declared as OUTPUT/BYPRODUCTS, consumed through declared dependencies; configure leaves no litter in the source tree); configure-time cost is the memory discipline: list operations stay in one scope to avoid quadratic copying, string(REGEX) never runs over unbounded input, and project data is never parked in the cache to keep it around.

security.best_practice: Consistent with Kitware's documented model: listfiles execute with the user's full authority, script mode is not a sandbox, and the download-pinning mechanisms (URL_HASH, full-commit GIT_TAG, OVERRIDE_FIND_PACKAGE) are the documented FetchContent controls. The guide's registry and PATH-poisoning cautions follow from the documented find_package/find_program search behavior.
security.evidence: Guide sections 18, 19 and 25 state the supply-chain rules per dependency class, the containment-check discipline (cmake_path IS_PREFIX and file(REAL_PATH) before comparison), and the staged-install rule that an install is never rehearsed against a real prefix.
security.guide_position: A configure step is code execution with the developer's credentials, so network at configure time is a declared, opt-in supply-chain event: every download is pinned by URL_HASH (SHA-256 or stronger) or a full commit hash, never a branch or floating tag; FetchContent runs behind OVERRIDE_FIND_PACKAGE so a reviewed system or vendored copy wins before any download; nothing fetched during a configure is included or executed in the same configure without a hash check in between; CI presets deliberately disable the package registries so a stray ~/.cmake/packages entry cannot redirect a dependency; secrets never enter the cache, a preset or a generated file; builds are out-of-source only, configure-time writes stay inside the binary dir, installs are staged into a scratch prefix first, and recursive deletes name a variable validated to be inside the build or staging directory in the same scope.

memory_ownership.guide_position: RAII and Rule of Zero; unique_ptr for exclusive ownership, shared_ptr only for genuine shared ownership, cycles broken deliberately; nonthrowing destructors; explicit checked finish for fallible completion; views borrow and never extend lifetime.

record.aspect_adaptations: All 10 aspects map directly onto C#; the adaptations are of mechanism, not of meaning: assertions_contracts is read against Debug.Assert being compiled out of Release builds (the C# analogue of Java's -ea model); memory_ownership is read as disposal ownership (IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable, one creator-disposer per resource) plus GC retention discipline (roots, caches, event handlers, rented buffers), since the GC owns reclamation; concurrency is read as async/Task discipline plus engine main-thread boundaries, which is where this estate's C# actually races.

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Microsoft's model is the guide's model: Debug.Assert is conditional on DEBUG and absent from Release, so it can only ever diagnose programmer invariants; boundary rejection belongs in explicit guard exceptions (ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull and siblings). Nullable flow analysis is static evidence, not a runtime boundary - Microsoft documents that deserialization/reflection can defeat it, as the guide states.
assertions_contracts.evidence: No .NET 10-era guidance changes assertion semantics or the ThrowIf* guard pattern; the guide's postconditions-are-tested-under-Release rule follows directly from the conditional-compilation fact.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: Debug.Assert for programmer invariants only - no mutation, authorization, or any needed side effect inside, because assertions are compiled out of Release. External input is rejected at the boundary with a precise exception (ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull, ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative, or a domain exception), guard clauses first so failure leaves state unchanged. Postconditions are documented and tested, including under Release configuration.

bounded_work.best_practice: No Microsoft source prescribes numeric budgets; nothing contradicts named bounds. The deferred-execution warning is core LINQ documentation behavior: an unmaterialized query re-runs per enumeration against possibly mutated state, which is why the guide's materialize-once-under-a-bound rule is the correct discipline.
bounded_work.evidence: Tiger policy stricter than mainstream by design; the guide names its bounds (ItemCountMax, PayloadSizeMaxBytes, DepthMax, MaxParallelism, retry count + shared deadline + backoff) and its reference module's executed cases (10 passed, per the commissioning record) exercise the count/total budgets at and past their limits.
bounded_work.guide_position: Every externally influenced size, count, duration, and fan-out gets a named PascalCase constant and a boundary rejection or clamp: item counts checked before allocation, byte payloads capped and streams read in bounded chunks (never ReadToEnd on untrusted length), every wait/retry/external call deadline-bound via CancellationToken, fan-out admitted through a bounded channel or semaphore, recursion over external data depth-capped. LINQ materializes once, at a named point, under a count bound. A retry without max attempts, shared deadline, and backoff is an unbounded loop.

concurrency.best_practice: Current Microsoft guidance is the guide's position: async all the way (blocking on .Result/.Wait() risks deadlock under a synchronization context and thread-pool starvation), ConfigureAwait(false) in library code with analyzer CA2007 enforcing it, CancellationToken flowed and honored, Task.Run reserved for CPU-bound offload, async void only for event handlers, ValueTask under its single-await consumption law.
concurrency.evidence: Nothing in the .NET 10 / C# 14 release changes async semantics in a way that relaxes any of these rules; the guide additionally handles the estate-specific boundary (engine coroutines/awaitables vs Task async crossed only at explicit adapters stating thread and cancellation owner), which platform guidance does not cover and does not contradict.
concurrency.guide_position: Async all the way to the entry point; never .Result, .Wait(), or .GetAwaiter().GetResult() outside a documented entry-point shim. One ConfigureAwait position per layer: libraries ConfigureAwait(false) (CA2007 under the house build), application/engine code captures its context deliberately. Every async API takes a CancellationToken last and honors it. Fire-and-forget is a decision with an owner (task stored, exceptions observed, lifetime bounded). lock regions are short, never span an await, and follow a stated order; shared mutable state has one owner and one stated discipline.

error_handling.best_practice: The guide's split is the documented idiom: exceptions for contract violations, TryX(out ...) for expected failures on hot/parsing paths, narrow catches, bare Exception only at top-level boundaries that log and translate, cause preserved (bare throw;, never throw ex;), and OperationCanceledException treated as control flow that propagates.
error_handling.evidence: No .NET 10 change alters exception or cancellation semantics; the async surfacing rule the guide documents (exceptions surface where the task is awaited) is the platform's stated behavior.
error_handling.guide_position: Contract violations throw precise exception types naming the rejected value's role (never secret content); expected failures return via TryX or a small result type. Catch only what the layer can interpret; empty catch forbidden; bare Exception only at a top-level boundary (process entry, engine callback root, message pump) that logs with context and translates or terminates by stated policy. Custom exceptions derive from Exception with standard constructors, sealed unless designed as a family base, few per subsystem.

Microsoft's guidance matches the guide's named failure modes - one long-lived HttpClient or IHttpClientFactory (per-call clients exhaust sockets), SafeHandle over hand-written finalizers, ArrayPool/MemoryPool rental with return on every path, and awareness of the ~85,000-byte large-object-heap threshold.

memory_ownership.guide_position: Whoever creates an IDisposable disposes it on every path (using / await using for IAsyncDisposable); ownership transfer is stated in the return documentation and visible in the API shape; disposal in own types is idempotent and safe on partially constructed objects. Retention is the leak model: event subscriptions pair += with -=, static fields and unbounded caches are roots with an eviction story, closures capturing this are named. Fast/large buffers rent from ArrayPool/MemoryPool and return on every path; hot structs stay small, with size assertions where per-frame/per-item counts are high.

security.best_practice: The guide's headline ban is now stronger than when such guides were first written: BinaryFormatter is obsolete as error (SYSLIB0011) and, since .NET 9, its runtime implementation is removed - the APIs throw for all project types, and Microsoft strongly recommends migrating away due to CWE-502 deserialization risk. Parameterized SQL, ArgumentList process launches, regex match timeouts, and XXE-safe XML settings (DtdProcessing prohibited, no external resolution) remain the documented controls.
security.evidence: Microsoft's own BinaryFormatter-removal post and the SYSLIB obsoletion index (checked 2026-10-14) confirm the guide's 'obsolete because unsafe-by-design' characterization and its ban; no current guidance relaxes the SQL, shell-string, or regex-timeout positions.
security.guide_position: Validate at the boundary, then trust inside - the boundary includes deserialization, reflection, P/Invoke, engine callbacks, and plugin/mod calls. Banned outright: BinaryFormatter and relatives, dynamic execution of external text, loading assemblies from untrusted paths without a stated trust decision. SQL parameterized always, including 'internal' queries. ProcessStartInfo with UseShellExecute=false and ArgumentList, never shell strings. unsafe blocks are small, commented with the invariant that makes them sound, and adversarially tested; P/Invoke crossings validate lengths, handles, and error codes. Secrets never in source, logs, exception messages, or fixtures.

record.aspect_adaptations: Build-definition adaptation: assertions_contracts = build-time verification (BuildKit build checks set to error, RUN checksum/version asserts, postcondition file checks); bounded_work = layer-count, image-size, context-size, and download retry/timeout budgets stated in the header and enforced in CI; concurrency = BuildKit stage-graph parallelism, cache-mount sharing modes, multi-platform builds, and bounded CI admission; memory_ownership = layer/image-size ownership (caches redirected to mounts or deleted in the same RUN, copies as allocation, parallel stages multiplying builder memory); static_analysis = pinned hadolint plus the builder's own checks and ShellCheck over embedded shell.

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the Dockerfile reference's own model: parser directives (syntax, check) are documented in the reference, the check directive exists since frontend v1.8.0, and BuildKit v0.34.0's release notes confirm build checks and provenance are maintained current features. Nothing official recommends warn-only checks for shipped artifacts.

assertions_contracts.guide_position: A build that cannot verify its assumptions fails at build time: input preconditions asserted in RUN (tool --version comparisons, sha256sum -c on downloads); BuildKit's lint checks are assertions - they warn by default, so the guide sets # check=error=true (check directive since frontend v1.8.0) and pins the frontend so new checks arrive only with a deliberate pin bump; output postconditions asserted before the final stage closes (binary exists and is executable, forbidden files absent via test ! -e); never assert by || true.

bounded_work.best_practice: No Docker source prescribes numeric budgets; bounding build work is the guide's policy layer on top of documented mechanics (context upload cost, cache retention via buildx prune --keep-storage), and nothing in the reference or BuildKit notes contradicts stated budgets enforced in CI.
bounded_work.evidence: The Dockerfile reference documents the instructions whose costs the budgets govern; the budget numbers themselves are labeled policy in the guide's Sources note.
bounded_work.guide_position: Budgets named in the header comment and enforced in CI: a reviewed layer-count budget for the final image, a maximum image size in MiB per artifact, a bounded build context (via .dockerignore, with an expected size class), work bounds inside RUN (downloads with capped retries and a timeout, e.g. curl --fail --retry 3 --max-time 300; package operations over a named finite set; loops over enumerated inputs only), and cache retention pruned on a stated --keep-storage ceiling; count and bytes are both bounded.

concurrency.best_practice: Consistent with BuildKit's documented execution model: independent stages build concurrently off the stage graph, cache mounts document shared vs locked sharing modes, and buildx --platform produces one manifest list per logical multi-platform build. The guide's cautions (memory multiplication, locked sharing for concurrent writers) follow from those same docs.
concurrency.evidence: buildx v0.37.2 (current stable, fetched in this pass) and BuildKit v0.34.0 notes describe the parallel/cache machinery the guide designs against; nothing newer changes the model.
concurrency.guide_position: Adapted as build parallelism and cache semantics: stage parallelism is the builder's, governed by the dependency graph, so stages are designed to be genuinely independent; cache mounts take sharing=locked for concurrent writers (default shared mode is for read-mostly caches); multi-platform builds are one logical build producing one manifest list, with QEMU emulation budgeted and native per-arch builders preferred; CI admission (N parallel image builds per runner) is a numbered resource decision.

error_handling.best_practice: Matches the builder's contract as documented: a failed instruction fails the build, and the reference's variable/exec-form semantics are what the guide's failure reporting assumes. No official guidance blesses suppressing instruction failures in shipped builds.
error_handling.evidence: The guide's failure-class split (input/build/environment) is its own reporting discipline layered on the documented fail-fast builder behavior; nothing consulted contradicts it.
error_handling.guide_position: A failed instruction fails the build - no || true, no downloads without --fail turning a 404 into an installed file; failures are reported by class (input failure: digest/checksum mismatch, the supply chain working; build failure: the code or script is wrong; environment failure: registry unreachable, secret not provided) because each has a different owner; retries belong only to idempotent network fetches with caps; builds stay side-effect-free beyond the image and cache so cleanup stays the builder's job.

formatting.guide_position: Honest position: there is no canonical Dockerfile formatter and the guide does not pretend otherwise - conventions are the formatter, enforced by review and pinned hadolint: one instruction per logical line with consistent continuation indent, uppercase instructions, lowercase stage names, package lists one per line in alphabetical order, blank lines between stages, directives grouped at the top, exec-form JSON arrays as valid double-quoted JSON; the Docker Language Server formats Compose and Bake files and lints/hovers Dockerfiles, and a floating linter is named a hazard (hadolint v2.15.0's new rules failed previously clean files the day it shipped - an argument for pinning).

memory_ownership.best_practice: Follows from the documented layer model (the reference and BuildKit docs agree layers are additive and deletions are whiteouts) - cache-in-layer and copy costs are the ecosystem's standard accounting, and COPY --link is a documented frontend feature for layer reuse.

memory_ownership.guide_position: Adapted as layer/image-size ownership: parallel stages multiply builder memory (capacity bug, not a retry opportunity); package caches are allocation with no owner - redirected to cache mounts or deleted in the same RUN that created them, since a later-layer deletion reclaims nothing; copies are allocation too (prefer COPY --link where the pinned frontend and base allow); the context upload is paid on every build, so the bounded context is a memory/time budget, not tidiness.

security.guide_position: Pin the builder and frontend, not just the bases (moby/buildkit by version/digest in driver-opts, # syntax= pin for the frontend); no secrets in any layer - not ENV (persists to runtime/children), not ARG (visible in history metadata), not copied-then-deleted - the one sanctioned path is a BuildKit secret mount supplied from the CI secret store; least privilege in the artifact (numeric non-root USER, read-only-rootfs-compatible design, minimal surface, setuid binaries removed where unneeded); downloads verified (ADD --checksum or fetch + sha256sum -c; curl | sh forbidden in all forms); bases from official/verified tiers with signature/attestation verification where the registry supports it; .dockerignore as a security boundary; HEALTHCHECK and EXPOSE explicitly not security controls.

record.aspect_adaptations: HTML is a document language with no compiler, runtime ownership, or threads of its own, so the matrix is adapted honestly: assertions_contracts = validator gates (vnu / SuperHTML / semantic lint) run on the assembled document; memory_ownership = DOM and resource-cost discipline (node/depth budgets, hidden-but-present content, template vs rendered markup, subresource lifetimes); concurrency = parser/render ordering and async loading semantics (defer vs async vs module scripts, resource hints, arrival-order independence); bounded_work = named document/resource budgets (bytes, DOM nodes, subresources, collection sizes rendered by producers); error_handling = designed failure appearances (missing CSS/scripts/images, error documents, broken links).

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the platform's own conformance model: the Living Standard defines authoring conformance requirements and the Nu Html Checker is the reference checker for them; because the parser recovers from every error, a validator gate on the assembled document is the only observable correctness signal. Nothing in current WHATWG or validator guidance contradicts the three-layer gate.
assertions_contracts.evidence: The validator project's own README confirms the release model the guide describes (rolling 'latest' artifact; 20.6.30 was the final numbered major release), and the Living Standard is the continuously updated target the guide names. SuperHTML's repo confirms it validates syntax, nesting, and attribute values against the living specification.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: Assertions are validator gates, not runtime checks: vnu zero errors on the assembled document is the primary gate, SuperHTML check adds a stricter second reading (stricter wins for hand-authored docs), and htmlhint/html-validate assert semantic invariants (labels, alt presence, heading order, unique ids, one main). Checker version is pinned/recorded; warnings are triaged.

bounded_work.best_practice: No official HTML source prescribes document budgets; nothing contradicts named budgets. Platform measurement tooling (browser devtools node/byte counts, Lighthouse's DOM-size audit) supports the guide's measure-it stance.
bounded_work.evidence: Tiger policy stricter than mainstream by design; the guide itself labels the numbers as project policy, not spec values, and names the measuring instruments.
bounded_work.guide_position: Named UPPER_SNAKE_CASE budgets declared per project and checked in the pipeline: DOCUMENT_BYTES_MAX 100 KB (compressed HTML), DOM_NODES_MAX 1,500, ELEMENT_DEPTH_MAX 32, SUBRESOURCE_COUNT_MAX 50, IMAGE_COUNT_MAX 30, FORM_CONTROLS_MAX 100, TABLE_CELLS_MAX 10,000 as starting values; every collection rendered into markup is bounded at the producer; third-party embeds count double and name an owner and failure appearance.

concurrency.best_practice: The Living Standard's script execution model matches the guide: defer scripts run in order after parsing, async scripts run on arrival, module scripts are deferred by default. Arrival-order independence and reserved geometry are the standard cure for load races and layout shift.
concurrency.evidence: Guide's defer/async/module statements restate the spec's execution-order rules; no newer loading primitive in the current standard displaces them (fetchpriority, which the guide uses for the single priority resource, is the current addition and is covered).
concurrency.guide_position: Markup sets the terms of the parser/network/render race: defer for ordered scripts, async only where order does not matter, module scripts preferred (deferred by default); content must not depend on arrival order of independent resources; resource hints spent sparingly (preconnect for the few origins that matter); third-party tags async or absent and never gating first paint or form submission; space reserved for late content.

error_handling.best_practice: Consistent with platform behavior and long-standing practice: documents degrade partially, so each failure mode (missing stylesheet, blocked script, missing image, error status) needs a designed appearance; a soft-404 misleads crawlers and users alike.
error_handling.evidence: No contradicting official guidance found; the guide's rules follow from the standard's parsing/rendering model (content survives without CSS/JS only if semantics carry it).
error_handling.guide_position: Every failure's appearance is designed in the contract: width/height reserve the image box so failure degrades to alt text in a stable layout; page stays legible without CSS and usable without scripts (forms still submit, details still opens); 404/410 are real pages served with the correct status (no soft-404, no redirect-to-home); broken internal links are pipeline failures; no inline onerror papering over missing assets.

formatting.best_practice: SuperHTML remains an actively maintained validator/formatter/LSP implementing the living specification; its current release line is v0.7.0 and its documented position is that the formatter accepts no configuration options - exactly the decree-formatter property the guide relies on.
formatting.evidence: The SuperHTML repo (README and v0.7.0 release notes, checked 2026-10-14) confirms the no-configuration formatter, the check/fmt/lsp commands the guide invokes, and continued releases; the guide's fallback chain (prettierd/prettier for templated contexts SuperHTML does not cover, exactly one formatter per file) matches SuperHTML's own stated templating limitation.
formatting.guide_position: One formatter per document class: SuperHTML for complete documents (no configuration by upstream design; superhtml fmt --check is the gate), with diver's prettierd/prettier/SuperHTML fallback chain for contexts outside SuperHTML's strict validation, never two formatters in sequence on one file. Explicit closing tags everywhere (omitted end tags flagged), double-quoted attributes, bare boolean attributes, void elements without the XHTML slash.

memory_ownership.best_practice: Adapted aspect (see aspect_adaptations): the DOM is the allocation the reader's machine pays for. Platform guidance (Lighthouse DOM-size audits, loading/fetchpriority semantics in the standard) supports node/depth discipline and deliberate resource lifetimes; nothing contradicts the guide.
memory_ownership.evidence: The guide's rules (flatten purposeless wrappers, do not ship hidden duplicate regions, template for inert markup, preload only what this page uses, preload=none for click-to-play media) are direct applications of the standard's loading model; no official source prescribes a different discipline.
memory_ownership.guide_position: The DOM is the memory model: node count and depth are the headline costs; wrapper divs carrying no semantics, styling hook, or script hook are packaging, not elements. Hidden-but-present content is still allocated - prefer not rendering, template elements, or server-side selection over shipping hidden variants. Subresource lifetimes are markup-controlled: lazy loading defers, preload is a scarce promise, media elements hold decoders/buffers, dynamic regions are bounded and emptied deliberately.

security.best_practice: Matches current platform security practice: context-sensitive output encoding, strict-CSP-compatible markup (no inline handlers), SRI for third-party subresources, least-privilege iframe sandboxing, and the documented allow-scripts + allow-same-origin sandbox escape the guide explicitly warns about. WCAG/ARIA guidance and the standard support the rest.
security.evidence: The sandbox-token trap, the four encoding contexts (text, attribute, URL, script - including the </script> breakout), and the SRI/crossorigin pairing are all stated in the standard and MDN's compatibility record the guide cites; no current guidance relaxes any of them.
security.guide_position: Encode by context at the boundary via the templating layer (text, attribute, URL, and script contexts each have a different regime; double-encoding is also a bug). No inline event handlers and no javascript: URLs without exception - markup a strict CSP would break is wrong markup. target=_blank is rare and always rel=noopener. Every iframe is titled and carries the least sandbox token set (the allow-scripts + allow-same-origin combination is called out as no sandbox). CDN scripts/styles carry SRI + crossorigin or are self-hosted; no secrets in markup; user-supplied markup is rendered as text or through a reviewed allowlist sanitizer.

static_analysis.best_practice: The three-layer stack (reference conformance checker, strict second reader, semantic/a11y lint) remains the current shape of HTML static analysis; SuperHTML v0.7.0 extended its diagnostics (ARIA attribute support among them) without changing the model, and html-validate continues to cover fragments/templates offline.
static_analysis.evidence: Tool currency verified 2026-10-14 against the projects' own repos/release pages; the guide pins/records checker versions and treats upgrades like compiler upgrades, which matches vnu's rolling-release model.
static_analysis.guide_position: Static analysis is the assertion stack of section 4: vnu (conformance), SuperHTML check (stricter spec reading incl. spec-legal-but-wrong markup), htmlhint/html-validate (semantic and accessibility invariants, fragment-aware), plus axe-core in testing. LSP pairing: vscode-html-language-server for general support, SuperHTML's LSP for strict validation; markuplint is in diver's linter set.

testing.best_practice: No official source prescribes a document test split; the guide's gates-on-assembled-output plus adversarial fixtures (injection per encoding context, malformed nesting, keyboard traps, contract violations, oversize inputs) matches how the platform's own test culture (web-platform-tests) treats conformance: behavior is checked against the assembled result, not author intent.
testing.evidence: The guide's own record for its reference document (vnu zero errors, SuperHTML clean, tidy 0 errors reported for the sample shape) is consistent with the suite it prescribes; no contradicting guidance found.
testing.guide_position: Half validation / half adversarial, run against the built, assembled site plus fragment unit checks: validation asserts all gates pass, links/fragments resolve, labels/alt/heading order hold, keyboard walk completes, budgets hold, pages render without CSS and function without scripts. Adversarial fixtures (malformed nesting, per-context injection, duplicate ids, second main smuggled by a component, unsandboxed iframe, GET form that mutates, oversize collections) must be rejected by the gates or survived inert; fixtures re-run on every toolchain upgrade.

record.aspect_adaptations: All 10 aspects map directly onto Java with no redefinition needed; the only adaptation is emphasis: memory_ownership is read as resource ownership plus JVM budget ownership (heap, metaspace, direct buffers, thread stacks, retention) since the GC owns reclamation, and assertions_contracts is read against the JVM's -ea model, where assertions are off in production launches by default.

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Unchanged JVM semantics: assertions evaluate only with -ea, production launches normally omit it, and Gradle Test / Maven Surefire enable assertions in tests by default - precisely the trap the guide names. JSpecify annotations remain tooling input, not runtime guarantees.
assertions_contracts.evidence: No JDK release through 27 changes assertion semantics; the guide's identical-behavior-with-and-without--ea rule and its reference module's executed checks (13/13 on three JDKs, per the commissioning record) are consistent with current platform behavior.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: assert only for programmer invariants, never for safe rejection, never with mutation or authorization inside; external values are rejected by an explicit precise exception, and behavior must be identical with and without -ea. Boundary validators with precise postconditions are preferred over annotation-plus-unchecked-cast.

bounded_work.best_practice: No official Java source prescribes numeric budgets; nothing contradicts named bounds. The platform direction supports the guide: bounded executors/queues and admission control in front of scarce resources remain the documented cure for spike-to-OOM failures.
bounded_work.evidence: Tiger policy stricter than mainstream by design; the guide derives limits from workload budgets, states exhaustion behavior per resource, and counts the runtime's own budgets (heap, executor queues, caches) as line items.
bounded_work.guide_position: Bound item count, item size, nesting depth, cumulative bytes, concurrent work, waiting work, elapsed time, and retry amplification separately, with named constants and a stated exhaustion behavior (example table: 1 MiB input, 1,024 items, depth 32, 8 active jobs, 64 queue entries, 3 attempts in one deadline, 256 KiB captured output per stream). Unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue and Executors.newCachedThreadPool are defects. Retries require idempotency, a shared deadline, bounded backoff, injected jitter. -Xms/-Xmx set deliberately.

concurrency.best_practice: The guide's preview discipline is exactly current: virtual threads are final since JDK 21 (JEP 444); JEP 491 (JDK 24) removed synchronized pinning of carrier threads; structured concurrency is still preview in JDK 27 (JEP 533, seventh preview, API still changing - join() exception typing changed this round), with finalization only proposed as JEP 543 (candidate) for JDK 28. Production contracts on stable APIs remain the correct posture.
concurrency.evidence: OpenJDK's JEP 533 page (checked 2026-10-14) confirms the seventh-preview status in JDK 27 and the per-round API changes the guide cites as its reason for not shipping --enable-preview contracts; JDK 27's GA feature list confirms the same.
concurrency.guide_position: Virtual threads (final, JDK 21) are the default for I/O-bound tasks - one task per thread, blocking style, never pooled, admission bounded by named semaphore/queue limits in front of scarce downstream resources; CPU work gets a bounded platform-thread executor. On the JDK 21 floor, synchronized blocks doing I/O inside virtual threads are a scalability defect (pinning; JEP 491 fixed it in JDK 24) - use ReentrantLock there. Structured concurrency's shape (one owner, one lifetime, cancellation propagates) is mirrored with ExecutorService + explicit deadlines; no preview APIs in production. Interruption is the cancellation protocol; shared mutation needs a checkable happens-before story.

error_handling.best_practice: No change in the platform's exception model through JDK 27 alters the checked/unchecked contract mechanism; the guide's policy is a deliberate, internally consistent use of it (checked = caller-actionable boundary condition, unchecked = programming error), with interruption handling per the concurrency APIs' own contracts.
error_handling.evidence: The guide's rules (never throws Exception/Throwable on public APIs, never catch-and-swallow, preserve causes, restore-or-propagate interrupt status, suppressed exceptions under try-with-resources, do not catch Error) match the JDK APIs' documented behavior; no official guidance contradicts the split.
error_handling.guide_position: Checked exceptions mark boundary conditions the immediate caller can act on; unchecked mark contract violations and bugs. Never catch-and-swallow; catch only what the layer can interpret; wrap with context and preserved cause. InterruptedException is a cancellation signal - restore the flag or propagate. Exceptions are not ordinary control flow (a not-found is a return value); a broad catch exists only at an outer boundary with logging, cleanup, and a defined failure response.

Downstream evidence also shows 1.37.0 changed a programmatic API (JavaFormatterOptions.Style became a record) that Spotless 8.10.3 calls, so the bump is not yet a drop-in for the guide's Spotless wiring - the pin may stay, the currency claim cannot.

Never run a second formatter or hand-wrap against its output.

memory_ownership.best_practice: The JVM model the guide states is current: try-with-resources with reverse-order close and suppressed cleanup failures, no reliance on finalization/Cleaner for correctness, and explicit budgets for heap/metaspace/direct buffers/stacks. JDK 27's default changes the guide flags (G1 default in all environments, JEP 523; compact object headers by default, JEP 534) are confirmed in JDK 27's GA feature list - the guide's 'pin and measure your own defaults' conclusion follows.
memory_ownership.evidence: JDK 27's shipped feature set (JEP 523, 527, 534, 536 final; checked 2026-10-14) matches the defaults the guide's memory section warns will move under applications; nothing in current OpenJDK guidance contradicts the one-owner rule.
memory_ownership.guide_position: Adapted aspect: one clear AutoCloseable owner per resource, exercised through try-with-resources in acquisition order; ownership transfers stated in Javadoc; finalization/Cleaner are leak detectors, not lifetime mechanisms. Allocation discipline: bound caches/buffers/retained chains/queued work; heap, metaspace, direct buffers, and per-thread stacks are explicit review items (a thousand platform threads are a memory commitment - one reason virtual threads are preferred for I/O); boxing in hot loops, per-call regex compilation, and static/listener/ThreadLocal retention are named leak shapes.

security.best_practice: Current platform guidance aligns with every prohibition: native deserialization of untrusted streams remains a code-execution boundary (JEP 290 filters are defense in depth), XML external entities stay off absent a reviewed contract, and JDK 27 adds in-process JFR data redaction (JEP 536, final) - which the guide already anticipates by name.
security.evidence: JDK 27's GA list confirms JEP 527 (post-quantum hybrid TLS key exchange) and JEP 536 (JFR redaction) as shipped finals, matching the guide's security section written before this audit; no official source relaxes the deserialization or XXE positions.
security.guide_position: Never deserialize untrusted Java-serialization streams; ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290) is defense in depth, not permission. XML parsers: DTDs/external entities disabled unless a reviewed contract requires them. Parameterized SQL; ProcessBuilder argv lists, never shell strings; validated URL schemes/destinations incl. redirects. The classpath is a trust boundary; reflection/setAccessible across modules is a privilege escalation to justify. Secrets never in logs, exception messages, command arguments, or unredacted JFR recordings.

static_analysis.best_practice: The guide's one-authoritative-policy rule remains the sane posture, and its nullness layer is current: JSpecify 1.0.0 defined the four consensus annotations (@Nullable, @NonNull, @NullMarked, @NullUnmarked), and 1.0.1 is a documentation/build-only follow-up with no semantic changes - so the guide's 1.0.x pin and its warning against legacy JSR-305/vendor annotation sets hold exactly.
static_analysis.evidence: JSpecify's own release notes (checked 2026-10-14) confirm 1.0.0's annotation set and 1.0.1's no-semantic-change status; Error Prone/NullAway and the Checker Framework remain the maintained checkers beyond annotations, as the guide presents them.
static_analysis.guide_position: Choose one authoritative static-analysis policy - JDT LS diagnostics plus Error Prone/NullAway or the Checker Framework for nullness beyond the JSpecify annotations - and explain genuine differences between tools instead of globally suppressing diagnostics. Null discipline: @NullMarked package default via package-info.java, @Nullable for exceptions, annotations checked at boundaries rather than trusted (Kotlin/reflection/native code do not read them).

testing.best_practice: JUnit 6 is the current JUnit line and requires a Java 17 baseline, which the guide's JDK 21 floor already exceeds; the 50/50 validation/adversarial split with boundary, overflow, exhaustion, cancellation, and assertions-disabled runs matches current practice. No newer runner displaces it in the guide's estate.
testing.evidence: The claim itself is consistent with the JUnit project's current line; however the guide's own citation for it ([J11]) points at an unrelated project's commit rather than a JUnit project page - a source-quality defect reported separately, not a verdict change: the runner choice and test discipline were verified, the in-guide citation was not primary.
testing.guide_position: JUnit is the runner (JUnit 6, Java 17 baseline). Tests split roughly evenly validation/adversarial: nulls where non-null is promised, null elements, false/zero, empty, maximum, one past maximum, oversize, wrong types at raw boundaries, negatives, integer overflow at the exact boundary, resource exhaustion. Boundary validation runs with assertions disabled as well as enabled. Concurrency tests cover timeout, cancellation/interrupt restoration, sibling failure, cleanup after failure, and stale generations. jqwik property tests use bounded generators and fixed seeds; every test has a timeout. Reference module: 13 executed cases.

Closed objects (additionalProperties: false) are stricter than the spec default, which is project policy, not a contradiction.

assertions_contracts.guide_position: Schema is the assertion system: schema written before or with the producer (never fitted to current output), every contract object closed with additionalProperties: false, every field typed and bounded (prefer enum/const over pattern), the draft pinned via $schema to Draft 2020-12, format asserted only when the validator is configured to assert it (annotation by default under 2020-12), and validation as a CI gate with a pinned validator that can fail the build.

bounded_work.best_practice: No JSON RFC prescribes numeric bounds, but RFC 8259 itself warns that implementations may set limits on numbers, strings, and nesting - bounding is the spec-sanctioned posture. The guide correctly separates contract bounds from tool limits: jq 1.8's internal ceilings (parsing depth raised to 10000, arrays/objects capped at 2^29) describe when jq falls over, not what a contract accepts.
bounded_work.evidence: RFC 8259 section 9 (parser limits) is the primary source for the bounds posture; the jq limits figures are the guide's reading of the jq 1.8.0 release notes in its J4 source, and jq 1.8.2 is confirmed as the current release in this pass.
bounded_work.guide_position: Named example bounds per contract - MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES (1 MiB), MAX_DEPTH (64), MAX_KEYS (256), MAX_ITEMS (10,000), MAX_STRING_BYTES (64 KiB) - enforced before or during parsing where the parser supports it, and a bound exceeded is a rejection with a named error, never a silent truncation.

concurrency.best_practice: No official JSON source defines a concurrent-write model for whole files; the guide's ordering (single writer, then append-only records, then lock+replace, then a database) matches how the ecosystem actually behaves - NDJSON's spec makes each line an independent complete text, which is what makes appends well-defined at all.
concurrency.evidence: The NDJSON specification (the guide's J5) defines the per-line complete-document property the append lane depends on; nothing in RFC 8259 sanctions read-modify-write on shared files.
concurrency.guide_position: Adapted to shared files: whole-document replacement does not compose under concurrency (two read-modify-write writers lose one update silently), so the guide orders the options - one writer per contract file; append-only NDJSON for record streams (single appender, or O_APPEND with line-sized writes and a stated platform assumption); lock + read-validate-modify-replace for the rest; genuinely multi-writer transactional data belongs in a database.

security.best_practice: The guide's positions are the primary sources' own: RFC 8259 section 4 says names SHOULD be unique and warns behavior with duplicates is unpredictable; I-JSON (RFC 7493) restricts interoperable documents exactly as the guide's profile does; JCS (RFC 8785) is the standards-track answer to hash/signature canonicalization; and jq's 1.8.2 release being largely security fixes (depth limits, NUL handling, hash-seed randomization) is the guide's stated reason for pin currency, with 1.8.2 confirmed current tonight.
security.evidence: RFC 8259 and RFC 8785 were the guide's J1/J3; the jq releases page (J4) confirms 1.8.2 as the current release line the guide names.
security.guide_position: Parser differentials are the core vulnerability: the strictest parser in a chain validates at the boundary and downstream re-parses only bytes the boundary emitted (or the chain standardizes on one parser+version); duplicate keys rejected with a detecting parser where available (jq does not detect them, so jq is never the only boundary gate); __proto__/constructor/prototype forbidden in JS-bound data with safe JS-side merging; JSON embedded in HTML escapes < so </script> cannot terminate the block, plus U+2028/U+2029 awareness; never assemble JSON by string concatenation; schema pattern regexes treated as a DoS surface (anchored, simple, or enum instead); secrets get 0600, no VCS, no fixtures.

bounded_work.guide_position: Named-constant bounds on every axis separately: input file bytes, enumerated items, recursion depth (Get-ChildItem -Depth), active jobs and -ThrottleLimit, Wait-Job -Timeout, total attempts within one shared deadline with bounded backoff and injected jitter, and captured output redirected to files and read back bounded; retries require idempotence; a pipeline stage that materializes input converts a streaming bound into a memory bound and must say which it relies on.

concurrency.best_practice: Consistent with the documented semantics: jobs and runspaces are separate sessions that do not inherit the caller's preference variables, and -ThrottleLimit is the documented admission control for ForEach-Object -Parallel and Invoke-Command. The guide's re-establish-the-contract rule is the documented-correct response to that isolation.
concurrency.evidence: Guide sections 13 and 21 state the isolation facts and the bounds; Microsoft's preference-variable documentation confirms preference state is per-session, which is exactly the hazard the guide designs against.
concurrency.guide_position: Four fan-out mechanisms compared by isolation and cost (Start-Job, Start-ThreadJob, ForEach-Object -Parallel, manual runspace pools); every fan-out is bounded by a named -ThrottleLimit and every wait by a timeout; state, StrictMode and $ErrorActionPreference are re-established inside each job/runspace and data crosses explicitly via $using: or -ArgumentList; per-worker errors are collected and inspected after the join; results re-enter in no promised order and are sorted or keyed before touching state.

error_handling.guide_position: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' at the top of every script and module plus explicit -ErrorAction Stop at trust boundaries; terminating vs non-terminating channels distinguished and the non-terminating channel treated as a trap outside per-item work; catch blocks name the expected exception or FullyQualifiedErrorId, add context, and rethrow or convert to a classified failure; a caught failure never exits 0; native commands are checked via $LASTEXITCODE captured in the very next statement, and on 7.4+ $PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true is enabled in strict scripts while keeping manual checks where nonzero codes carry information; every CI-invoked script ends with a deliberate documented exit code.

memory_ownership.guide_position: One clear owner per file handle, .NET stream or client, job, runspace pool, CIM/remoting session and temporary file; IDisposable objects are disposed in finally (PowerShell has no using statement, so finally is the contract); sessions and jobs are removed by the code that opened them; cleanup failure is reported, not swallowed; retention is bounded deliberately: materializing pipeline stages, $Error accumulation, -Raw reads and whole-graph JSON loads are named costs, and fan-out payloads are counted per runspace (paths and identifiers cross boundaries, not payloads).

record.aspect_adaptations: systemd unit files are declarative supervisor configuration, not a programming language, so the matrix is adapted honestly: assertions_contracts is read as unit-file verification and contract checking (Condition vs Assert semantics, ExecStartPre contract checks, systemd-analyze verify as the gate); memory_ownership is read as resource-control and state-ownership discipline (cgroup v2 MemoryHigh/MemoryMax/TasksMax ceilings, slice budgets, and the directory directives as the ownership mechanism for state, cache, logs and runtime paths); concurrency is read as service parallelism and ordering semantics (parallel activation unless After/Before orders it, dependency-graph transactions, slice activating-concurrency, socket activation, restart-storm desynchronization); static_analysis is systemd-analyze (verify plus the security exposure audit), there being no separate type system or linter for unit files.

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the documented semantics in systemd.unit(5): conditions skip quietly, assertions fail the unit, and systemd-analyze condition evaluates both before anything starts. Postconditions stated in the unit and checked by tests is stricter than common practice, not contradicted by it.
assertions_contracts.evidence: Guide section 4 states the two failure semantics and the checks-not-setup rule for ExecStartPre; section 28 makes verify warnings gate failures via --recursive-errors=, which is what turns the contract into a checkable assertion.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: Condition... directives express genuine optionality (a failed condition skips the unit quietly and successfully); Assert... directives express deployment-guaranteed preconditions (a failed assertion marks the unit failed); ExecStartPre commands are cheap, fast, read-only contract checks that fail the start early and loudly, never setup or migration; postconditions are stated in Description/Documentation and verified by the testing split (socket answers after start, no cgroup process survives a stop, a timer elapse ran its service or its skip is explained by a condition).

bounded_work.best_practice: Consistent with systemd.resource-control(5) and systemd.unit(5): every axis the guide names is a real directive with the stated exhaustion behavior, and the start-limit defaults the guide cites (5 bursts per 10 s) are systemd's own manager defaults. Requiring the budget to be stated rather than inherited is Tiger policy, stricter than default.
bounded_work.evidence: Guide section 5 tabulates the axes with directives and exhaustion behavior, and the reference unit in section 31 states its budget (StartLimitBurst=5, StartLimitIntervalSec=10min) in [Unit], where the directives belong.
bounded_work.guide_position: Every forever gets a stated budget per axis: MemoryMax (hard) and MemoryHigh (soft), CPUQuota, TasksMax, LimitNOFILE set deliberately rather than to maximum, StartLimitBurst per StartLimitIntervalSec in [Unit] plus RestartSec, RuntimeMaxSec for runs that must end, WatchdogSec with sd_notify, TimeoutStartSec/TimeoutStopSec, journald rate limits understood, and StateDirectoryQuota and peers (v258+) for directory growth; values are derived from measured appetite plus headroom with the derivation commented, never copied from another unit, and infinity is a review finding wherever it appears.

concurrency.best_practice: Matches the manager's documented model: activation is parallel wherever the declared graph allows, ordering and requirement are separate axes, and socket activation removes the readiness race. The two 262 additions the guide names are real: v262 release coverage and the upstream commit record RestartRandomizedDelaySec, and the same coverage records slice ActivatingConcurrencyMax.
concurrency.evidence: The official v262 release (tagged 2026-09-22) is the current upstream release; the upstream commit adding RestartRandomizedDelaySec describes it as the restart-storm desynchronization mechanism the guide's section 21 presents, and release coverage of v262 confirms ActivatingConcurrencyMax on slices and the static PID 1 build.
concurrency.guide_position: Boot and transaction order is parallel by default and only declared After/Before ordering serializes it; a starting unit does not queue a second copy of an already-active unit, which is the non-overlap guarantee for oneshot self-overlap, while sibling overlap is the program's lock (flock) and the unit names that fact; slices are the concurrency budget for a class of work, with v262's ActivatingConcurrencyMax capping simultaneous activations in a slice; restart storms are desynchronized with RestartSec jitter (RestartRandomizedDelaySec, v262) and staggered RandomizedDelaySec; socket activation is the concurrency-friendly shape, with Accept per-connection instances only for genuinely stateless programs.

error_handling.best_practice: The exit-status, OnFailure and stop-escalation model matches systemd.service(5) and systemd.kill(5), and KillMode=none is indeed deprecated upstream (since v246 the manager warns that it disables process lifecycle management). One current mechanism improves on the guide's reload contract: the latest systemd.service(5) defines Type=notify-reload, expects RELOADING=1/READY=1 notifications around a manager-sent reload signal, and recommends it over a signal-based ExecReload for services that support reloading, even verifying the reload-signal handler is installed; the guide's section 20 presents ExecReload (typically /bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID) as the reload contract and never mentions notify-reload.
error_handling.evidence: The current systemd.service(5) text fetched for this audit describes notify-reload in detail and states that using it with the reload protocol is the efficient, recommended alternative to providing an ExecReload command for signal-reloadable services; guide sections 7 and 20 contain no occurrence of notify-reload.
error_handling.guide_position: Exit status policy is declared (SuccessExitStatus, RestartForceExitStatus, RestartPreventExitStatus) with a preference for fixing the program's codes; OnFailure wires important failures to a unit a human will see and OnSuccess covers oneshot completion hooks; stop behavior is SIGTERM, TimeoutStopSec sized for real drain work, then SIGKILL to the cgroup (SendSIGKILL default on); KillMode stays control-group by default, mixed is the named middle case, and process/none abandon the stop guarantee and need a written reason (none is deprecated upstream); start failures land in failed and are never papered over with ExecStartPost tricks or - prefixes on commands whose failure is the signal.

formatting.best_practice: True as stated: systemd ships no canonical unit formatter and no estate-wide third-party one has standing; verification plus consistent house conventions is the honest maximum. Nothing in the current upstream documentation announces a formatter the guide is missing.
formatting.evidence: Guide section 23 states the absence plainly instead of inventing a tool, and sections 27/28 give the validation recipes (verify, calendar, security) that substitute for a format gate.
formatting.guide_position: No canonical formatter exists and the guide does not invent one: the discipline is one directive per line, no trailing whitespace, file ends with a newline, section order [Unit] then the type section then [Install], blank line between sections, directives alphabetized within a section except where order is semantics (dependency sequences, Exec lines in run order), rare indented continuations, values unquoted unless they contain spaces or comment characters, full-line comments only, suffixed time/size values, and yes/no boolean spelling throughout; in the editor, systemd_ls diagnostics assist but formatting stays a reviewed-diff discipline.

memory_ownership.best_practice: Consistent with the cgroup v2 resource-control model in systemd.resource-control(5): accounting is on by default under v2, MemoryHigh and MemoryMax are distinct tools, and OOMPolicy has existed since v243. The v258 facts the guide builds on are real: v258 removed cgroup v1 support and added per-directory storage quotas.
memory_ownership.evidence: Guide sections 5, 14 and 15 state the accounting-first discipline and the directory lifetimes; v258's removal of cgroup v1 and its per-service directory quotas are confirmed in the v258 release record, and the systemd.exec(5) source the guide cites carries the per-directive version records (directory directives 211, quotas 258).
memory_ownership.guide_position: Memory control is accounting first, limits second: MemoryAccounting defaults on under cgroup v2, usage is measured before any ceiling is set, MemoryHigh (reclaim pressure) sits below MemoryMax (the hard cgroup OOM wall) when growth is the risk, MemorySwapMax bounds swap, OOMScoreAdjust is a documented relative statement, and OOMPolicy=stop is the usual Tiger choice so an OOM'd unit enters the failure machinery; state ownership belongs to the directory directives, whose lifetimes are explicit (RuntimeDirectory removed at stop unless preserved, State/Cache/Logs/Configuration directories persist and are removed deliberately via systemctl clean, and under DynamicUser the persistent dirs live under private/ parents so recycled UIDs cannot reach a prior tenant's state); slice membership gives a class of work a collective budget above the per-unit ceilings.

security.best_practice: The checklist reflects the current systemd.exec(5) sandboxing surface, and the guide's warnings are the documented ones: most filesystem sandboxing is unavailable to the per-user manager alone and takes effect there only combined with PrivateUsers, sandbox layers degrade silently where the kernel or container lacks the mechanism, and an unknown directive is logged and silently does nothing, which verify exists to surface. LoadCredential's credential-directory boundary and the world-readability of unit files are documented facts.
security.evidence: Guide sections 18, 19 and 26 state the policy, the per-directive mechanisms with their breakage modes (including the MemoryDenyWriteExecute/JIT warning), and the verify-on-target discipline; the exposure gate it prescribes (security --offline with --threshold, v250+) is the documented CI form.
security.guide_position: Sandbox by default from the section 26 checklist, weakening only on paper with a comment naming the workload fact: least user (dedicated or DynamicUser), NoNewPrivileges, empty-then-rebuilt CapabilityBoundingSet, PrivateDevices, PrivateNetwork or declared address families, ProtectSystem=strict with the directory directives as the writable exception, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, the ProtectKernel/ControlGroups/Clock/Hostname family, ProtectProc=invisible with ProcSubset=pid, LockPersonality, MemoryDenyWriteExecute piloted per service because it blocks JIT runtimes, SystemCallFilter with SystemCallErrorNumber=EPERM, RestrictNamespaces, UMask=0077; secrets never travel in Environment (world-readable files, systemctl show, /proc environ) and go through LoadCredential/LoadCredentialEncrypted or a 0600 EnvironmentFile; systemd-analyze security exposure at or below the unit's agreed threshold is the gate, with the review covering what the score cannot see.

static_analysis.best_practice: systemd-analyze is the documented analysis surface for unit files: verify checks unit files and their references, and the security subcommand's offline mode with a threshold is the documented CI gate (both since v250 for the offline/threshold forms). static_analysis.guide_position: The gate toolchain is systemd-analyze: verify clean with --recursive-errors= set so warnings (unknown directives, missing binaries, bad references) fail the run instead of passing silently; security run offline with an agreed --threshold and non-zero exit above it; calendar used to normalize and preview every OnCalendar expression; systemd_ls provides editor diagnostics and directive completion in Neovim, but no formatter or DAP adapter is claimed, because none exists.

record.aspect_adaptations: Data-format adaptation: assertions_contracts = schema-as-contract (yamllint style rules, JSON Schema / consumer schemas such as kubeconform, consumer-side re-validation); bounded_work = document bytes, keys, depth, alias count and post-expansion size bounds (the billion-laughs class); concurrency = concurrent writers of shared YAML state, multi-document stream semantics, and CI serialization via Actions concurrency groups (documents themselves do not execute); memory_ownership = parser memory discipline measured on the expanded document, streaming vs DOM loading, and the extra cost of comment-preserving round-trip parsers; static_analysis = the pinned linters/validators (yamllint, yaml-language-server, actionlint, zizmor, kubeconform).

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the specification ecosystem's own model: the YAML 1.2.2 spec defines resolution and uniqueness but leaves semantic contracts to schemas, and JSON Schema (2020-12, still the latest released draft) is the standard contract language; consumer-side validation at the boundary is the documented defense against validator/consumer disagreement.
assertions_contracts.evidence: The 1.2.2 specification (opened directly) states mapping-key uniqueness and core-schema resolution in the sections the guide cites; json-schema.org still names 2020-12 as the current version.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: Schema validation is the assertion system, in three layers: yamllint (syntax/style, --strict) first, then a schema (JSON Schema, or the consumer's own - kubeconform for Kubernetes, actionlint+zizmor for Actions), then consumer-side re-validation at the runtime boundary; a document class without a schema gets one before it grows a second consumer; a document failing any layer is rejected whole.

bounded_work.best_practice: No official YAML source prescribes numeric budgets; the guide's alias bound has direct precedent in a shipping parser - the JavaScript yaml package caps alias resolution (maxAliasCount, default 100) explicitly to prevent exponential entity expansion. Stricter-than-default project bounds are policy, not contradiction.
bounded_work.evidence: The eemeli/yaml options documentation lists maxAliasCount with default 100 and describes it as preventing exponential entity expansion attacks - the exact precedent and number the guide's section 5 cites.
bounded_work.guide_position: Named example bounds per document class: document bytes (256 KiB hand-written / 1 MiB generated), documents per stream, keys per mapping (128), nesting depth (20), aliases per document (100, fan-out <= 10), expanded size <= 10x source with an absolute cap, scalar length (8 KiB); bounds enforced by the parser during resolution, not after allocation; compressed input judged on expanded size.

concurrency.best_practice: Consistent with GitHub's own Actions guidance, which provides concurrency groups to serialize runs against shared environments, and with the one-writer/atomic-replace discipline the format's tooling assumes; no official source prescribes last-writer-wins for shared manifests.
concurrency.evidence: GitHub's security-hardening guidance for Actions (the guide's Y2) is the primary source for the workflow-side rules; nothing in it or the spec contradicts the one-writer position.
concurrency.guide_position: Adapted to a data format: shared YAML state gets one writer or an explicit format-aware merge step; atomic rename makes a single write indivisible but does not make two writers agree, so multi-writer state carries a version/checksum key; deploy workflows must serialize with Actions concurrency groups - omitting one is a concurrency decision by omission.

error_handling.best_practice: Matches the specification's own failure model (well-formedness, identified aliases, resolved/recognized tags are distinct failure points in section 3.3 of the spec) and standard validator practice; no official source recommends proceeding past a parse failure with substituted data.
error_handling.evidence: The 1.2.2 specification's loading-failure-points section separates the failure classes the guide separates; the guide adds gate policy on top, which is its prerogative.
error_handling.guide_position: Four distinct failure classes handled distinctly - parse errors (reject, naming file and line), lint errors (reject at the gate under --strict), schema errors (reject whole, naming the key path), consumer errors (the consumer's contract) - with fail-closed behavior throughout; a silent fallback to a default/empty document on parse error is named an anti-pattern, and a fallback is legitimate only as an explicit, reviewed, logged document.

formatting.best_practice: Consistent with the tools' own documentation: prettier's options page documents the 80-column default the guide warns against inheriting silently, and yamllint documents itself as a linter with style rules (including key-duplicates and truthy) rather than a rewriting formatter.
formatting.evidence: The guide's citations for both claims are the tools' official pages (yamllint changelog/repo, prettier options); yamllint 1.38.0's changelog confirms the rule set (indentation, quoted-strings, key-ordering) is actively maintained as documented.
formatting.guide_position: 2-space indent, spaces never tabs (tabs are illegal YAML indentation), block style by default, flow only for short leaf collections; one pinned formatter per repository (yamlfmt in this estate; prettier where the stack is JavaScript, with print width set explicitly because prettier's default is 80); yamllint is a linter, not a formatter, and the two configs are kept in agreement; a formatter check must be idempotent and load/dump round-trips are not editing.

memory_ownership.best_practice: Matches the parser ecosystem's documented behavior: the JS yaml package's alias cap exists because expansion is where the memory goes, and ruamel.yaml's reason to exist (comment preservation) is documented to be a different, heavier processing model than PyYAML's load/dump.
memory_ownership.evidence: eemeli/yaml's options doc ties maxAliasCount to exponential-expansion prevention; the guide's parser matrix (section 26.1) records the same per-parser behavior the projects document.
memory_ownership.guide_position: Adapted as parser-memory discipline: the memory a document costs is its expanded size, not its file size (alias expansion multiplies nodes geometrically, modeled in section 38 as E ~ b^d); streaming parsers reduce peak memory only while the consumer stays incremental; a comment-preserving round-trip parser holds the token stream as well as the value and costs more than a bare loader - the right trade for editing tools, the wrong one for a hot loading path.

security.best_practice: This is GitHub's and PyYAML's own documented guidance: PyYAML's wiki warns yaml.load on untrusted data is as powerful as pickle.load and made the Loader argument mandatory in 6.0; GitHub's security-hardening doc and Security Lab research prescribe the env: indirection, minimal permissions, and SHA pinning the guide mandates; the Sept 2025 anchors changelog confirms anchors/aliases are supported on GitHub.com while merge keys remain rejected, exactly as the guide's section 26.2 states.
security.evidence: The GitHub changelog of 2025-09-18 (the guide's Y4) is the anchors source; independent Oct 2026 write-ups confirm merge keys still produce errors in Actions. PyYAML's deprecation wiki is the safe-loader source.
security.guide_position: Safe loaders only for external input (custom tags rejected, not ignored; FullLoader is not a middle ground); anchor bombs bounded at the parser; validator/consumer disagreement (duplicate keys, 1.1-vs-1.2 scalar typing) treated as an exploit shape with one dialect and duplicate rejection as mitigations; no secrets in documents; Actions discipline: explicit minimal permissions block, actions pinned to full-length commit SHAs, untrusted ${{ }} expressions reach run: only via env:, pull_request_target/workflow_run treated as privileged triggers.

proposals.proposal: Re-baseline the guide to Zig 0.17.0 as a migration pass, not a pin swap: re-run the section 31 reference module under 0.17 (replace '**' with @splat), sweep sections 2/19/20/26/27 for build, process, Io and std renames, re-point sources [Z1]/[Z2] at the 0.17.0 documentation set, and record the ZLS state honestly (0.17-matched ZLS not yet stable; editor diagnostics degraded until the Build Server Protocol lands)
proposals.recommendation: Adopt as the next Zig guide pass; until it lands, the guide must be read as a 0.16.0 guide - its internal discipline holds at that pin

proposals.evidence: Carried forward from run 1 (not applied; pass-2 addendum leaves all per-language proposals open): the toolchain's test/build system includes fuzzing of test inputs in both 0.16 and 0.17; the guide's testing section relies solely on enumerated boundary cases, the exact weakness fuzzing addresses for parsers
proposals.proposal: Add Zig's built-in fuzzing (zig build test --fuzz / fuzzable test cases) to the testing workflow for byte parsers and decoders, alongside the existing Debug/ReleaseSafe/ReleaseFast matrix.
proposals.recommendation: Adopt for parser-shaped code; keep the enumerated boundary matrix as the deterministic gate and treat fuzzing as a corpus-growing supplement.
